newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian officials under fire on radio licenses.
newsitem.headline: Colombian officials under fire on radio licenses.

text.p: Two top Colombian officials came under heavy political and legal fire on Monday after a leaked tape indicated they might have illegally awarded radio broadcast licenses to cronies of President Ernesto Samper.

This week's edition of the top political magazine Semana published a transcript of part of a conversation between the ministers of communications and of mines and energy recorded in July. The transcript shows the Cabinet members discussing how to divide up some of the 81 new FM broadcast licenses among the "president's friends."

"The idea is that at least half (the licenses) should be for (the president's) friends, the ones who we already know," Communications Minister Saulo Arboleda told Mines Minister Rodrigo Villamizar in the tape, said to have been recorded on or about July 21.

"Fifty percent for others and 50 percent for friends of the president. We will see how we distribute them (the licenses)," Villamizar replied, according to the Semana report. The pair talked in detail about two broadcast licenses in the southwestern city of Cali, Villamizar's hometown.
The government directly awarded the contracts on July 24 after two bidding processes were voided because of a lack of investor interest.
Juan Camilo Restrepo, leader and presidential candidate of the opposition Conservative Party, termed the brewing scandal "another blow to press freedom" and called for the two ministers to be fired.

"This had undermined press freedom less than a year before the elections," he told reporters. "President Samper should fire them both before the matter is passed to Congress. I shall be asking Congress today to start impeachment proceedings against both."
Previous opposition-sponsored motions of political censure against members of the Cabinet have failed because Congress is dominated by Samper's ruling Liberal Party.
Chief Prosecutor Alfonso Gomez and Attorney General Jaime Bernal both said they would launch an official investigation into the way the radio licenses were awarded.

In a brief statement, Villamizar, a key member of Samper's Cabinet who has just returned from hospital treatment in the United States, conceded he had had an informal chat with Arboleda. But he added, "I never suggested taking any personal part in the process of awarding FM broadcast licenses."

Indications of shady dealings in awarding the licenses came less than a month after Colombia's constitutional court upheld a controversial new television law. Under the law, all program makers will have to submit new bids for broadcast slots, a requirement that opponents fear could lead to anti-government news shows being taken off the air.
Such a move, critics believe, could greatly boost the chances of Samper's chosen successor, former Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, in presidential elections next May.
